description: Hi! I’m focused, love reading, and I’m strong in science. Our team is made up of top-ranked students who are creative, skilled, and enjoy building fun projects that perform well. We’re looking for a strong coder to join us and aim for the top prize together!
summary: Our team created an interactive mini-game website about past NASA missions and the rovers and spacecraft they used. Many of these machines are still out there. Spirit is still sitting in the sand on Mars, Apollo 11's equipment is still on the Moon, and Pioneer 10 is still flying away from the Sun. We really wanted these missions to be recognized by the public, and to do that we needed to get their attention. Honestly, no one likes to read a webpage full of just words and pictures. So instead of a boring, word-filled website, we made a game. You draw a random explorer, learn where it is now, and play through its mission. At big moments you decide what NASA should do, like whether Opportunity should keep driving or wait out a dust storm, and then you see what NASA really chose. Three wrong calls and your mission is lost. Finish it, and the explorer is added to your collection. We all researched different missions and their machines, and based on our research, our group leader built the website. There are 17 explorers to collect, each with a real NASA 3D model or photo.
details:
1) What it is

1 in a Galaxy is a browser game that tells the stories of 17 retired NASA explorers on the Moon, on Mars, and in deep space. Instead of reading a list of facts, the player lives through each mission and makes the same hard choices NASA had to make.

2) How it works

1. Draw: Press the button and a random explorer is picked, like opening a card pack.

2. Explorer card: See where it is right now, when it launched, how it got power, and its "family" (its twin, the rocket it rode on, the teams that built it).

3. Mission timeline: The mission plays forward in fast time. When a key moment comes, the game stops and gives you 3 choices. Every choice has a good side and a bad side, so there is no obvious answer.

4. Compare with NASA: After you pick, the game shows what NASA actually did and explains why.

5. Win or lose: 3 wrong choices and the mission explodes. Finish the mission and the explorer goes into your collection book.

6. Collect all 17: Each explorer has a real NASA 3D model you can spin around, or a real NASA photo if there is no model.

3) Explorers in the game

Moon: Apollo 11, Apollo 12 ALSEP, Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle, Surveyor 3

Mars: Viking 1, Viking 2, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Phoenix, InSight, Ingenuity

Deep space: Pioneer 10, Pioneer 11, Dawn, NEAR Shoemaker, Kepler

4) Secret stage

There is a hidden stage with a 1% chance of showing up. In it, you become NASA and plan your own mission with 18 decisions: power, heat, radio, rocket, launch weather, route, landing, and how to come home. Your budget and weight are limited, so you cannot pick the safe option every time. Then you watch your spacecraft launch and fly in 3D. If it fails, the game tells you about a real NASA mission that failed for the same reason, like the Mars Climate Orbiter and its unit mix-up.

5) Why it matters

These spacecraft are part of history, but once they go silent most people forget them. Making a decision and then seeing what really happened sticks with you much longer than reading about it. Our game is free, runs in any browser, works on phones, and has English and Korean, so students can use it at home or in class.

6) What makes it creative

- You don't just learn about a mission, you play it and can fail it.

- No choice is the obvious right one. Each one has a real trade-off.

- The random draw and collection book make people want to come back and find the rest.

- The 3D models and photos are real NASA material, not made-up pictures.

7) What we considered

- Accuracy: Each member researched different missions, and we checked dates and facts against NASA mission pages and the NSSDCA archive.

- Difficulty: We rewrote the choices many times because the first versions were too easy to guess.

- Speed: The NASA 3D models were very large, so we compressed them and split them into smaller files so the site loads in a normal browser.

- Ease of use: A short tutorial explains the game the first time you play.

8) Tools

HTML, CSS, JavaScript, three.js (3D models), Web Audio API (music and sound effects), glTF-Transform and Blender (to shrink the NASA 3D models), GitHub Pages (hosting)

9) Team

Team Fayston: Minjun, Zion, Jio, Justin, Hoyon
